newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan's Lee conducts high-profile military review.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan's Lee conducts high-profile military review.

text.p: President Lee Teng-hui on Monday reviewed a display of Taiwan's newly beefed-up arsenal, kicking off high-profile war games seen by some as provocative ahead of rival China's takeover of Hong Kong.

Bolstering Taipei's message of defiance, Lee's inspection tour was aired live on Taiwan television and witnessed by 200 foreign journalists -- ensuring the message would project across the Taiwan strait to Taiwan-watchers in the mainland.
Taiwan has said that the timing of its two-day "Chinese glory" drills, announced a year ago, had nothing to do with Britain's midnight, June 30, handover of Hong Kong to Beijing.

Commanders made clear, however, that the drills had everything to do with China and its intensifying drive to isolate the exiled Republic of China, which retreated to Taiwan after losing a civil war to the communists in 1949.

"This exercise can show our countrymen the military's accomplishment in breaking through the obstacles of military procurement and their success in domestic weaponry research and development," the defence ministry said in a statement.
Beijing, which views Nationalist-ruled Taiwan as a renegade province, has warned other countries against arming the island in its drive to bring it under mainland rule.
Lee inspected a host of high-tech imported arms, including U.S. F-16 and French Mirage 2000-5 jet fighters, AH-1W attack helicopters and OH-58D surveillance helicopters.

The most innocuous-looking yet sophisticated weapons on show were the long, boxy truck-mounted launchers containing U.S.-made Patriot antimissile missiles -- procured to shoot down incoming missiles in the event of attack by mainland China.

Lee, flanked by vice president Lien Chan and military brass, nodded in satisfaction as he passed the drab green Patriots -- which at US$1 million each were not scheduled to be fired in Tuesday's live-fire war games.
The Patriots, along with advanced U.S. Hawk missiles and a range of Taiwan-developed missiles, have become the cornerstone of Taiwan's second-generation defence network.
Also on display were some of the 300 ageing M60A3 tanks that Taiwan bought on the cheap from the U.S. scrap heap -- only to upgrade them with the latest electronic anti-aircraft systems.
The two-day manoeuvres have been seen by some as provocative because their timing comes so close to Hong Kong's handover.
Beijing has declined to be drawn, however.

Beijing's official Xinhua news agency issued a commentary on Sunday that hailed Hong Kong's return to China under a "one country, two systems" model of local autonomy as an example for Taiwan's own "reunification with the motherland".
The commentary made no mention of the Taiwan war games.

Similarly, Beijing's spokesmen have passed up many chances to condemn the manoeuvres, reinforcing analysts' belief that China wants to avoid rhetorical mudslinging that might spoil Hong Kong's shining moment.
Beijing also has declined to comment on unconfirmed Hong Kong media reports that it would respond with "counterbalancing" manoeuvres, something military analysts said was unlikely.
The United States gave voice to international concerns about the timing of Taiwan's drills, urging the sides on June 11 not to stage exercises during the run-up to Hong Kong's handover.
Taiwan rejected the U.S. advice, saying the military exercises had nothing to do with the handover.
